about: What to Notice: guided looks at a painting, one detail at a time. Written for this app from general art-history knowledge, not by the MFA. Regions are fractions of the picture: x, y, width, height. Pictures: Wikimedia Commons (public domain).

general.title: How to Look at a Painting
general.subtitle: Seven questions that work for any picture

steps.title: First, just look
steps.text: Give it a full minute before reading anything. What do you notice first? What feeling does it give you? Your first impression is a clue: the artist planned it.

steps.title: Composition and lines
steps.text: Find the big shapes: triangles, diagonals, verticals. Diagonals feel like movement; horizontals feel calm. Where is the centre, and what did the artist put there?

steps.title: Follow the eyes
steps.text: Where are the people looking: at each other, at something, at you? Painters use gazes and pointing hands like arrows to steer your eye around the picture.

steps.title: Light
steps.text: Where does the light come from, and what does it fall on? The brightest spot is usually the most important part. Shadows can hide, soften or add drama.

steps.title: Colour
steps.text: Which colour repeats? A strong colour (often red or blue) can tie the picture together or mark the main figure. Warm colours come forward; cool ones recede.

steps.title: Symbols and small details
steps.text: Look in the corners and the background. Objects often mean something: a skull for death, a lily for purity, a dog for loyalty. Painters hide stories in details.

steps.title: Context
steps.text: Who made it, when, and for whom? A church, a family, a market? Knowing the purpose explains a lot. Now look again: you’ll see more than the first time.

steps.title: First look
steps.text: Saint Luke, believed to have painted the first portrait of the Virgin, kneels to draw her while she nurses the baby Jesus. Rogier van der Weyden painted it in Brussels around 1435–40.

steps.title: Two worlds
steps.text: The room in front is sacred and enclosed. Through the columns opens an everyday world: a city, a river, boats. The picture joins the holy and the ordinary.

steps.title: The two figures with their backs to us
steps.text: Right in the centre, a small couple leans on the parapet and looks away, into the distance. They are our stand-ins: they turn us around and lead our eye out of the room. Some scholars think they are Mary’s parents, Joachim and Anna; that’s an interpretation, not a certainty.

steps.title: Follow their gaze
steps.text: Their gaze runs down the river to the horizon, the vanishing point of the picture. The whole composition funnels you there, a trick borrowed from Jan van Eyck’s Madonna of Chancellor Rolin, which has the same couple at the same parapet.

steps.title: The artist at work
steps.text: Luke draws with a silverpoint on paper, exactly how painters made studies in Rogier’s day. Luke was the patron saint of painters, and many think Rogier gave him his own face.

steps.title: Queen and mother
steps.text: Mary sits low, on the step, beneath a rich canopy of honour: a queen, yet humble. Nursing the child makes her tender and human, the ‘Virgin of the Milk’.

steps.title: Luke’s study
steps.text: Through the doorway at right is Luke’s study: an open book on the desk and, half hidden in the shadow below, an ox, the symbol of Saint Luke the Evangelist.

steps.title: Why it was made
steps.text: It was probably painted for the painters’ guild in Brussels, a portrait of their patron at work. Painters copied it for centuries; versions survive in Munich, St Petersburg and Bruges.

steps.title: First look
steps.text: The four daughters of Edward and Mary Boit in their Paris apartment, painted by Sargent in 1882. Notice how strange it is for a family portrait: nobody poses together.

steps.title: A square, an empty centre
steps.text: The canvas is square, and its centre is a dark, empty hallway. Sargent pushes the girls to the edges and into the shadows, like a snapshot of a quiet moment.

steps.title: Youngest, in the light
steps.text: Julia, about four, sits on the rug with her doll, full in the light and looking straight at us.

steps.title: Mary Louisa, standing apart
steps.text: Mary Louisa, about eight, stands alone against the wall, hands behind her back, also meeting our gaze.

steps.title: The two eldest, half lost
steps.text: Jane, twelve, and Florence, fourteen, stand deep in the shadow; Florence turns away and leans on a vase. As the girls get older, they recede. Many read it as a picture about leaving childhood behind; that’s an interpretation.

steps.title: The giant vases
steps.text: The towering Japanese vases dwarf the girls. They travelled with the family across the Atlantic and are now in the MFA too, displayed near the painting.

steps.title: Little sparks of light
steps.text: A mirror glints in the dark at the back, and a red screen flashes at the right. Sargent learned from Velázquez’s Las Meninas, another painting of children in a deep, shadowy room.

30998.file: J S Copley - Watson and the Shark (Boston).jpg

steps.title: First look
steps.text: Havana harbour, 1749: a shark attacks 14-year-old Brook Watson while his shipmates try to save him. Copley painted the true story in 1778, frozen at its most dramatic second.

steps.title: A triangle of people
steps.text: The rescuers form a pyramid, with the harpooner at its peak. This classic, stable shape holds the chaos together.

steps.title: The harpoon
steps.text: The harpooner is about to strike. His weapon’s diagonal points down at the shark’s open jaws, connecting attacker and defender.

steps.title: The shark
steps.text: Copley had probably never seen a shark: notice its odd lips and the nostrils. It still reads as pure menace.

steps.title: Watson in the water
steps.text: Watson floats on his back, pale, hair streaming, his hand reaching for help. He lost his right leg below the knee, though he survived and later became Lord Mayor of London.

steps.title: The sailor with the rope
steps.text: A Black sailor at the centre holds the rope that will reach Watson. Rare for 1778, a Black man is a key, heroic figure in a history painting, though we don’t know who he was.

steps.title: The real harbour
steps.text: Behind them is Havana, with its Morro Castle. Copley built the view from prints and maps: he had never been to Cuba.

33556.file: Claude Monet-Madame Monet en costume japonais.jpg

steps.title: First look
steps.text: Camille Monet, the painter’s wife, poses in a theatrical red kimono among Japanese fans. Monet painted it in 1876, at the height of Paris’s craze for all things Japanese.

steps.title: The blond wig
steps.text: Camille had dark hair. The blond wig makes clear she’s a Parisienne playing dress-up, not a Japanese woman.

steps.title: The fan she holds
steps.text: Her fan is in the French national colours, blue, white and red, a playful French touch in the middle of all the Japonisme.

steps.title: The samurai on the robe
steps.text: An embroidered warrior seems to burst out of the fabric, drawing his sword, almost a second figure in the painting. MFA research with colleagues in Japan linked the robe’s design to a Japanese story about samurai.

steps.title: The fans on the wall
steps.text: Look at the fans: some show faces of Japanese women, as if watching Camille. The wall behind turns into a pattern, flattening the space like a Japanese print.

steps.title: The train of the kimono
steps.text: The heavy, padded hem sweeps across the floor in a long curve: Monet paints the embroidery with thick, quick strokes you can almost touch.

steps.title: Then and now
steps.text: It was a success at the 1876 Impressionist exhibition; Monet later called it a potboiler. Today it also prompts questions about cultural appropriation, debated at the MFA in 2015.

steps.title: First look
steps.text: A blazing sunset over a stormy sea. Only slowly do you see what is happening in the water. Turner exhibited it in 1840 with the title: Slavers Throwing Overboard the Dead and Dying, Typhoon Coming On.

steps.title: The ship
steps.text: On the left, the ship sails on into the storm, leaving behind what its crew has thrown overboard.

steps.title: The sun
steps.text: The sun burns at the centre like a wound, its red reflected in the water. Beauty and horror are painted with the same brush.

steps.title: In the water
steps.text: At lower right, a shackled leg rises from the waves, circled by fish and gulls. Turner was thinking of the Zong massacre of 1781, when a crew threw enslaved Africans overboard to claim insurance.

steps.title: Chains and hands
steps.text: More chains and reaching hands float in the foreground, nearly dissolved into paint. The longer you look, the more you find.

steps.title: Why 1840
steps.text: Britain had abolished slavery in its colonies, but the trade went on elsewhere. Turner showed this in the year of the first World Anti-Slavery Convention in London.

32558.file: Gauguin - Where Do We Come From? What Are We? Where Are We Going? (1897-98).jpg

steps.title: First look
steps.text: Gauguin’s largest painting, made in Tahiti in 1897–98, which he called his testament. It is read from right to left, like a story of a human life.

steps.title: Where do we come from?
steps.text: At the far right lies a sleeping baby, watched by three women: the beginning of life.

steps.title: What are we?
steps.text: In the centre, a young figure reaches up to pick fruit: daily life, desire, perhaps the fruit of knowledge from the Garden of Eden.

steps.title: The idol
steps.text: Behind, a blue idol raises its arms, seeming to point to a world beyond. Gauguin described it as pointing to the Beyond.

steps.title: Where are we going?
steps.text: At the far left, an old woman crouches, hands to her face, near the end of life. At her feet, a strange white bird, which Gauguin said stood for the futility of words.

steps.title: The title in the corner
steps.text: Gauguin painted the title himself on a yellow patch in the upper left corner, as if on a worn fresco on a gold ground.

31601.file: Jean-François Millet - The Sower - Google Art Project.jpg

steps.title: First look
steps.text: A peasant strides down a hill at dusk, scattering seed. Millet painted it in 1850; at the Paris Salon some saw it as a political statement about the rural poor.

steps.title: A giant figure
steps.text: The sower fills almost the whole canvas, tilted on a strong diagonal, so he seems to stride toward us. Millet gives an ordinary labourer the size and dignity of a hero.

steps.title: The hand
steps.text: His open hand flings the seed in a wide arc: one gesture, repeated thousands of times a day.

steps.title: No face
steps.text: His face is lost in the shadow of his hat. He isn’t a portrait of one man but every man who works the land.

steps.title: The crows
steps.text: Black birds swoop in the sky at left, ready to eat the seed: the hard truth that not everything sown will grow.

steps.title: Far away
steps.text: On the bright horizon, a farmer works the field with oxen. The sower walks down from the light into the dark earth.

steps.title: Its long life
steps.text: Van Gogh copied this painting again and again, and the publisher Simon & Schuster made the sower its logo.

32542.file: Vincent van Gogh - Portret van de postbode Joseph Roulin.jpg

steps.title: First look
steps.text: Joseph Roulin, Van Gogh’s friend in Arles, painted in 1888 in his postal uniform. Look at how much character fits into one seated figure.

steps.title: The cap
steps.text: POSTES, written in gold across his cap. Roulin worked at the post office at the Arles railway station; he was proud of the job and the uniform.

steps.title: The beard
steps.text: His great forked beard is painted in curling strokes of many colours. Van Gogh compared him to Socrates.

steps.title: Blue on blue
steps.text: Dark blue uniform, pale blue background, gold buttons: Van Gogh uses a few strong colours instead of shadows and depth, an idea learned from Japanese prints.

steps.title: The hands
steps.text: Big, worker’s hands rest on the chair and table, slightly awkward, completely real. They make the official uniform human.

steps.title: A friendship
steps.text: Van Gogh painted every member of the Roulin family. When he was hospitalised after cutting his ear in December 1888, Roulin looked after him.

steps.title: First look
steps.text: Augustine Roulin, wife of Van Gogh’s friend the postman, painted in Arles in early 1889. Van Gogh made five versions of this picture.

steps.title: The rope
steps.text: In her hands is a cord. It rocks a cradle we can’t see, her baby daughter Marcelle, just outside the picture.

steps.title: Her face
steps.text: Calm, a little tired, outlined in dark paint. She doesn’t look at us; she is listening for the baby.

steps.title: The flowered wall
steps.text: Behind her, big flowers float on a green ground. The wall is flat as wallpaper: no depth, just pattern, an idea Van Gogh took from Japanese prints.

steps.title: Red and green
steps.text: Green skirt against red floor and chair: opposite colours that make each other glow.

steps.title: A lullaby for sailors
steps.text: Van Gogh imagined it hanging in a fishermen’s cabin, comforting men at sea, and once pictured it between two of his Sunflowers, like an altarpiece.

33278.file: Houses at Auvers by Vincent Van Gogh.jpg

steps.title: First look
steps.text: Cottages in Auvers-sur-Oise, painted in 1890, in the last weeks of Van Gogh’s life, when he made around 70 paintings in about ten weeks.

steps.title: Thatched roofs
steps.text: The old roofs are painted in long, thick strokes that look like the straw itself, mossy green and gold.

steps.title: One red roof
steps.text: A bright orange-red roof cuts through the greens and blues: the hottest colour, placed right where your eye lands.

steps.title: The sky
steps.text: Even the clouds are solid: curls of white paint you could almost lift off the canvas.

steps.title: A small figure
steps.text: In the lane, a tiny person walks by. Look how few strokes it takes to make a human being.

steps.title: The lane
steps.text: The path is painted in rippling blue and white strokes, more like water than earth. Nothing in this picture stands still.

steps.title: First look
steps.text: A rocky ravine near the asylum of Saint-Rémy, where Van Gogh lived in 1889–90. He painted it outdoors on a windy day.

steps.title: Rocks like waves
steps.text: The cliffs are drawn in long, flowing lines, so the stone seems to move like water.

steps.title: The stream
steps.text: At the bottom, a mountain stream twists through the gorge, a pale path that pulls your eye down.

steps.title: A small palette
steps.text: Blues, greens and greys, with a few flicks of orange for the plants: Van Gogh builds the whole scene from a handful of colours.

steps.title: Painting in the wind
steps.text: According to his letters, the mistral was so strong he had to hold the easel down with stones. You can feel that energy in every stroke.

33610.file: Vincent van Gogh - Weaver - Google Art Project.jpg

steps.title: First look
steps.text: A weaver at his loom in Nuenen, in the Netherlands, painted in 1884, before Van Gogh moved to Paris and his colours brightened.

steps.title: The weaver
steps.text: The man sits deep inside the wooden frame of the loom, almost a prisoner of his machine.

steps.title: The red cloth
steps.text: The one bright note in a brown, grey room: the red cloth on the loom, the work of his hands.

steps.title: The spinning wheel
steps.text: On the left, a spinning wheel: thread first, then cloth. The whole process sits in one room.

steps.title: A long study
steps.text: He made at least 28 paintings, drawings and watercolours of weavers, fascinated by the machinery and by the people working long hours for little pay.

35481.file: Vincent van Gogh - Enclosed Field with Ploughman - Google Art Project.jpg

steps.title: First look
steps.text: The walled wheat field Van Gogh saw from his window at the asylum in Saint-Rémy, painted in autumn 1889.

steps.title: The ploughman
steps.text: A man and his horses turn the earth, small against the huge field: the cycle of work and seasons Van Gogh loved.

steps.title: The windmill
steps.text: Far away, a windmill on the hill, a tiny vertical in a world of horizontal stripes.

steps.title: Furrows
steps.text: The ploughed earth runs in bands of violet, grey and yellow, painted with short strokes that follow the furrows.

steps.title: The hills
steps.text: Behind, the blue Alpilles hills and a pale sky close the view, like the wall around the field.

steps.title: First look
steps.text: A summer field near Monet’s home at Giverny, painted in 1890: poppies, poplars, distant hills.

steps.title: The poplar
steps.text: One tall, thin poplar splits the sky, a vertical accent in a picture made of horizontal bands.

steps.title: The poppies
steps.text: Red dabs scattered across green: complementary colours, side by side, seem to vibrate.

steps.title: Blue distance
steps.text: The far hills turn blue and pale. Monet paints air itself: things look bluer the farther away they are.

steps.title: The sky
steps.text: Pink-edged clouds in a pale sky: probably late in the day, when the light turns warm.

steps.title: First look
steps.text: Monet’s water-lily pond at Giverny, painted in 1907. There is no shore and no horizon, only the surface of the water.

steps.title: An upside-down world
steps.text: Look into the water: the pale shapes are reflections of the sky and trees. We look down, but we see up.

steps.title: Depth from lily pads
steps.text: The pads get smaller and closer together as they recede: that’s all Monet needs to make the pond feel deep.

steps.title: The flowers
steps.text: Each blossom is just a few touches of pink and white.

steps.title: The signature
steps.text: Claude Monet 1907, signed in the water itself, at lower right.

steps.title: His own garden
steps.text: Monet had the pond dug in 1893 and spent nearly 30 years painting it, about 250 canvases in all.

31803.file: Claude Monet - Flower Beds at Vétheuil - Google Art Project.jpg

steps.title: First look
steps.text: Monet’s garden at Vétheuil, above the Seine, painted in 1881. The flowers rise up almost to the river.

steps.title: Sunflowers
steps.text: Tall sunflowers stand out against the far bank, their yellow heads catching the light.

steps.title: A boat on the river
steps.text: Tiny on the water, a boat with a figure: easy to miss, it tells you the scale of the view.

steps.title: The island
steps.text: A wooded island sits in the river, softened by haze.

steps.title: A wall of colour
steps.text: Up close, the garden is a crowd of thick, round dabs: red, orange, green. From a step back they turn into flowers.

steps.title: First look
steps.text: A summer meadow with poplars, painted by Monet around 1875 near Argenteuil, outside Paris.

steps.title: The poplars
steps.text: Two dark trees fill the left side, holding the composition like a frame.

steps.title: A small figure
steps.text: In the long grass, a tiny figure in white with a straw hat, almost swallowed by the meadow.

steps.title: Poppies
steps.text: Red poppies flicker in the foreground: a few strokes of red make the whole field come alive.

steps.title: The sky
steps.text: Big white clouds in blue, painted quickly, the way they move on a windy day.

32103.file: Claude Monet - Rouen Cathedral Façade and Tour d'Albane (Morning Effect) - Google Art Project.jpg

steps.title: First look
steps.text: Rouen Cathedral early in the morning, painted in 1894. Monet made more than 30 views of this façade from rooms he rented across the square.

steps.title: The tower in light
steps.text: The Tour d’Albane catches the first sun and glows pale pink.

steps.title: The façade in shadow
steps.text: The rest of the front is still in cool blue shadow. Light, not stone, is the real subject.

steps.title: Paint like stone
steps.text: Look at the surface: layers of thick, crusty paint, as rough as the carved stone itself.

steps.title: The signature
steps.text: Signed and dated ’94 at lower left. Monet finished the series in his studio at Giverny.

steps.title: First look
steps.text: The same cathedral, from the same spot, at another hour. The MFA has two of Monet’s Rouen Cathedrals; compare them.

steps.title: The rose window
steps.text: The great round window is a dark, warm circle at the centre of the façade.

steps.title: The portals
steps.text: At the bottom, the doorways glow orange where the sun reaches into them.

steps.title: Crusted paint
steps.text: The paint is so thick it looks carved, built up over many sessions.

steps.title: A slice of sky
steps.text: Only a little blue sky shows at the top: the cathedral fills almost the whole canvas.

32183.file: Claude Monet - Poppy Field in a Hollow near Giverny - Google Art Project.jpg

steps.title: First look
steps.text: Poppies in a hollow near Giverny, painted in 1885.

steps.title: A river of red
steps.text: The poppies spill down the slope in a wedge of red, pulling your eye from the front up into the hollow.

steps.title: The hollow
steps.text: The hills fold around the field like cupped hands, closing the view.

steps.title: Dark bushes
steps.text: A few dark bushes act as stepping stones across the slopes.

steps.title: White flowers
steps.text: At lower left, white flowers in shadow: a cool note against all that red.

34078.file: Claude Monet, Haystack, Morning Snow Effect (Meule, Effet de Neige, le Matin), 1891, oil on canvas, 65 x 92 cm, Museum of Fine Arts, Boston.jpg

steps.title: First look
steps.text: A grainstack in snow, painted in 1891, one of about 25 grainstacks Monet painted near his house at Giverny across seasons and times of day.

steps.title: The stack
steps.text: Huge and simple, almost a mountain. Monet chose a dull subject so the light would be the real story.

steps.title: Blue shadows
steps.text: The shadow on the snow is blue and violet, not grey or black. Look at real snow on a sunny day: Monet was right.

steps.title: A rim of light
steps.text: The sun catches the top and edge of the stack in warm gold.

steps.title: The far trees
steps.text: A band of blue trees and houses closes the horizon, all in the same cold winter light.

steps.title: Signature
steps.text: Claude Monet ’91, lower left.

31792.file: Pierre-Auguste Renoir - Grand Canal, Venice - 19.173 - Museum of Fine Arts.jpg

steps.title: First look
steps.text: The Grand Canal in Venice, painted by Renoir in 1881 on his first trip to Italy.

steps.title: Gondolas
steps.text: Black gondolas glide across the shimmering water, the darkest shapes in the picture.

steps.title: Water made of dabs
steps.text: The canal is a mosaic of small strokes: blue, white, yellow. Up close it’s abstract; from a step back it sparkles.

steps.title: The palaces
steps.text: The palaces on the left melt into warm pinks and golds in the sunlight.

steps.title: Mooring poles
steps.text: The striped mooring poles at right lead your eye down to the water.

steps.title: Signature
steps.text: Renoir signed and dated it ’81 at lower right.

steps.title: First look
steps.text: A spring pasture painted by Camille Pissarro in 1889, when he was experimenting with the dot technique of Seurat and Signac.

steps.title: Woman and goat
steps.text: A peasant woman leads a white goat: the human scale of this calm landscape.

steps.title: Made of dots
steps.text: Look closely: the grass is built from small, separate touches of colour that mix in your eye.

steps.title: The cottage
steps.text: A steep roof and a red chimney peek over the hedge, the only building in the scene.

steps.title: The tree
steps.text: A big tree on the left, its leaves shimmering in dots of green, violet and yellow.

31454.file: Two Peasant Women in a Meadow (Le Pré).jpg

steps.title: First look
steps.text: Two peasant women resting in a meadow at Éragny, painted by Pissarro in 1893.

steps.title: The two women
steps.text: One sits, one stands, both turned away from us, part of the landscape rather than posing for it.

steps.title: The poplars
steps.text: Tall poplars rise like columns at the left, leading your eye up into the sky.

steps.title: The village
steps.text: Through the trees, a church spire and roofs: the village of Éragny, where Pissarro lived.

steps.title: Cows in the distance
steps.text: Far away in the field, a few cows graze, tiny touches of colour.

31810.file: Camille Pissarro - Morning Sunlight on the Snow, Eragny-sur-Epte - Google Art Project.jpg

steps.title: First look
steps.text: Morning sun on snow at Éragny, painted by Pissarro in 1895, looking out from his house.

steps.title: A lone walker
steps.text: A small figure trudges through the snow, the only movement in a frozen morning.

steps.title: A screen of trees
steps.text: Bare trees cover the whole picture like a veil you look through.

steps.title: Snow is not white
steps.text: The snow is made of pinks, violets, yellows and blues. That’s how sunlight looks on snow.

steps.title: Signature
steps.text: C. Pissarro ’95, lower left.

32190.file: Camille Pissarro - Sunlight on the Road, Pontoise - Google Art Project.jpg

steps.title: First look
steps.text: A sunlit road at Pontoise, painted by Pissarro in 1874, the year of the first Impressionist exhibition.

steps.title: Rider on a white horse
steps.text: A horseman rides along the road, the brightest shape on the left.

steps.title: A woman and a child
steps.text: A woman in a white cap walks with a small child toward the trees: everyday life, not a posed scene.

steps.title: Shadows on the road
steps.text: Long shadows cross the road: you can feel the low sun and the time of day.

steps.title: The trees
steps.text: Big trees on the right frame the scene and filter the light into dapples.

steps.title: The village
steps.text: Roofs of Pontoise peek out behind the greenery.

steps.title: First look
steps.text: Racehorses at Longchamp, near Paris, painted by Degas in 1871 and possibly reworked in 1874.

steps.title: Seen from behind
steps.text: Most of the horses walk away from us. Degas loved unusual angles, as if we just happened to be standing there.

steps.title: The jockeys’ silks
steps.text: Pink, yellow, blue and brown: the bright racing silks are the only strong colours on the grey-green field.

steps.title: A sudden gallop
steps.text: At left, a group breaks into a run, blurred with motion.

steps.title: The empty foreground
steps.text: The whole bottom half is empty grass. Degas leaves space, like a photograph taken at the wrong moment, on purpose.

32250.file: Edgar Degas - At the Races in the Countryside - Google Art Project.jpg

steps.title: First look
steps.text: At the races in the countryside, painted by Degas in 1869. It was shown at the first Impressionist exhibition in 1874.

steps.title: A family outing
steps.text: Degas’s friend Paul Valpinçon drives the carriage; his wife, the baby and a nurse sit behind. The race is almost an afterthought.

steps.title: The dog
steps.text: A little black dog perches on the carriage seat, looking out.

steps.title: Cut off
steps.text: The horses are sliced by the right edge, like a snapshot. Degas loved this cropping, borrowed from Japanese prints and early photography.

steps.title: The race, far away
steps.text: The actual race is a tiny scene in the distance on the left.

32372.file: Manet, Edouard - The Execution of Emperor Maximilian, 1867.jpg

steps.title: First look
steps.text: The execution of Maximilian, the Austrian archduke made emperor of Mexico by Napoleon III, shot in June 1867. This is the first of Manet’s versions.

steps.title: The victims
steps.text: At left, Maximilian and his two generals blur into the gunsmoke, barely there.

steps.title: The firing squad
steps.text: The soldiers stand in a tight line, faceless, their rifles a row of dark diagonals.

steps.title: The soldier apart
steps.text: At right, a bearded soldier stands calmly with his rifle, apart from the others. In later versions he readies the final shot.

steps.title: The smoke
steps.text: A cloud of white smoke hangs over the scene: the moment of the volley.

steps.title: Unfinished on purpose?
steps.text: The loose, sketchy paint makes it feel like news, raw and immediate. French censors kept the final version out of public view.

32912.file: Madame Cézanne dans un fauteuil rouge, par Paul Cézanne.jpg

steps.title: First look
steps.text: Hortense Fiquet, Cézanne’s wife, in a red armchair, around 1877. He painted her some 29 times.

steps.title: Her face
steps.text: Still, almost a mask. Cézanne cared less about expression than about solid forms.

steps.title: The red armchair
steps.text: The chair wraps around her like a big red shell, the strongest colour in the picture.

steps.title: The hands
steps.text: Folded calmly in her lap, the centre of the whole composition.

steps.title: The striped skirt
steps.text: Vertical stripes of green and blue run down like pillars, building her like architecture.

steps.title: The wallpaper
steps.text: Small blue motifs on the wall behind her, flat pattern against solid form.

steps.title: First look
steps.text: Early snow on a village street at Louveciennes, near Paris, painted by Alfred Sisley around 1870.

steps.title: The road
steps.text: The road sweeps into the picture and curves away: your eye walks down it.

steps.title: Two figures
steps.text: Two people walk along the snowy edge of the road, small and dark.

steps.title: Snow on the roofs
steps.text: Thin snow on the roofs and chimneys: the first snow of the season, not deep winter.

steps.title: The fence
steps.text: A wooden fence at right, half buried in white, leads back toward the houses.

steps.title: A quiet painter
steps.text: Sisley, born in Paris to British parents, painted the villages around Paris all his life, often the same roads Monet and Pissarro painted.

34222.file: Paul Gauguin - Paysage avec la femme bretonne Deux.jpg

steps.title: First look
steps.text: Two Breton women resting in a landscape, painted by Gauguin in Brittany in 1889, before he left for Tahiti.

steps.title: The two women
steps.text: One sits, one bends forward, both absorbed in their own thoughts.

steps.title: White caps
steps.text: The white coiffes, the traditional Breton headdresses, are the brightest spots in the painting.

steps.title: The twisting tree
steps.text: A long, bent trunk crosses the whole picture like a line in a drawing.

steps.title: Flat colour
steps.text: Big flat areas of yellow, green and pink, outlined with dark lines: Gauguin was moving away from Impressionism toward colour for its own sake.

steps.title: First look
steps.text: A windswept tree on the cliffs at Trouville, on the Normandy coast, painted by Monet in 1881.

steps.title: The tree
steps.text: One tree leans hard against the wind, its crown pushed sideways. It is the only character in the picture.

steps.title: Its bent trunk
steps.text: The thin trunk slants like a dancer: you can feel the wind that shaped it.

steps.title: The sea
steps.text: The sea is a calm, pale band behind the tree, almost the same colour as the sky.

steps.title: Grass in the wind
steps.text: The grass is a tangle of quick strokes in every direction, moving like the tree.

steps.title: Signature
steps.text: Claude Monet signed at lower right.

31042.file: Winslow Homer - The Fog Warning - Google Art Project.jpg

steps.title: First look
steps.text: A fisherman rows his small dory back to his ship off the coast of Maine, with a heavy catch. Winslow Homer painted it in 1885.

steps.title: The look over his shoulder
steps.text: He turns to look back at something: that glance is the story.

steps.title: The fog bank
steps.text: What he sees: grey fog rolling in from the horizon. If it reaches him before he reaches his ship, he’s lost.

steps.title: The schooner
steps.text: Far off, tiny on the horizon, the schooner he must row back to.

steps.title: The catch
steps.text: Big halibut lie in the boat: a good day’s work, and heavy weight in a rising sea.

steps.title: The waves
steps.text: The dory rides high on a rolling wave. Homer lived by the sea at Prouts Neck, Maine, and painted it from long watching.

steps.title: First look
steps.text: Night on a ship. An old sailor on watch calls out ‘All’s well’ while the bell rings the hour. Homer painted it in 1896.

steps.title: The face
steps.text: Weathered, bearded, mouth open mid-call, lit by a light we can’t see.

steps.title: The bell
steps.text: The ship’s bell, glinting in the dark, rings out the hours of the watch.

steps.title: Rope and rigging
steps.text: Ropes cut across the left side: we are right on deck with him.

steps.title: The night sky
steps.text: A dark blue sky with a few faint stars: a long, cold watch.

30881.file: Samuel Adams by John Singleton Copley.jpg

steps.title: First look
steps.text: Samuel Adams, Boston Patriot, painted by Copley around 1772. It was commissioned by John Hancock.

steps.title: The pointing finger
steps.text: He points firmly at a document on the table: the Massachusetts charter, which guaranteed the colony’s rights.

steps.title: The papers
steps.text: He holds a petition, and the charter lies with its seal. Copley recalls the moment after the Boston Massacre of 1770, when Adams demanded the governor remove British troops.

steps.title: His face
steps.text: Stern and direct. Copley shows a man of conviction, not of fashion.

steps.title: A plain suit
steps.text: No lace, no gold: a simple red suit against a dark background, the image of a man of the people.

steps.title: First look
steps.text: John Hancock, Boston’s richest merchant, painted by Copley in 1765, about ten years before he signed the Declaration of Independence.

steps.title: The account book
steps.text: Hancock rests his hand on a huge ledger: he wanted to be seen as a man of business.

steps.title: The quill
steps.text: Pen in hand, as if we interrupted him at work.

steps.title: The coat
steps.text: A fine blue coat with gold braid: wealth, shown with taste.

steps.title: His face
steps.text: Young (he was 28), calm, looking straight at us.

steps.title: First look
steps.text: Joseph Warren, Boston doctor and Patriot leader, painted by Copley around 1765.

steps.title: His face
steps.text: Young and open. Ten years later Warren was killed at the Battle of Bunker Hill, in 1775.

steps.title: The papers
steps.text: He rests his hand on papers on the table, the sign of an educated professional.

steps.title: The red curtain
steps.text: A rich red curtain at right, a standard way to give a sitter grandeur.

steps.title: The pose
steps.text: Seated, relaxed, one arm on the table: Copley’s portraits make people look natural, not stiff.

31228.file: John Singleton Copley - Mr. and Mrs. Ralph Izard (Alice Delancey) - 03.1033 - Museum of Fine Arts.jpg

steps.title: First look
steps.text: Ralph and Alice Izard, a South Carolina couple on their Grand Tour, painted by Copley in Rome in 1775, his first big portrait after leaving America.

steps.title: The Colosseum
steps.text: Through the window: the Colosseum. It tells you exactly where they are.

steps.title: The statue
steps.text: A classical sculpture group behind them, the kind of art Grand Tourists came to Rome to see.

steps.title: The drawing
steps.text: They discuss a drawing on the table, perhaps of the sculpture: the couple as connoisseurs.

steps.title: The Greek vase
steps.text: An ancient Greek vase at upper left, another sign of taste and learning.

steps.title: The gilded table
steps.text: A heavy carved and gilded table between them: luxury, and a divider between husband and wife.

31294.file: John Singleton Copley - Mrs. Richard Skinner (Dorothy Wendell) - 06.2428 - Museum of Fine Arts.jpg

steps.title: First look
steps.text: Dorothy Wendell Skinner of Boston, painted by Copley in 1772.

steps.title: The reflection
steps.text: Look at the polished table: her arm and sleeve are reflected in the mahogany. Copley was famous for these mirror-like surfaces.

steps.title: Hand to chin
steps.text: A thoughtful pose, finger at her cheek, as if lost in thought.

steps.title: The silk dress
steps.text: Shimmering silk, lace and a pink bow: Copley paints each fabric so you can almost feel it.

steps.title: Her cap
steps.text: A delicate lace cap on her piled-up hair, the fashion of the 1770s.

32171.file: John Singleton Copley - Venus and Cupid - 25.94 - Museum of Fine Arts.jpg

steps.title: First look
steps.text: Venus and her son Cupid, painted by Copley around 1779, after he moved to London and turned to mythology.

steps.title: Two faces, one embrace
steps.text: Cupid hugs his mother, cheek to cheek. Both look straight out at us.

steps.title: Cupid’s look
steps.text: A mischievous little smile: the god of love knows what he’s doing.

steps.title: Loose brushwork
steps.text: Look at the background: quick, sketchy strokes of blue and white, a free side of Copley rarely seen in his portraits.

steps.title: First look
steps.text: Christ rising to heaven while his apostles watch, painted by Copley in Rome in 1775, one of his first grand religious paintings.

steps.title: Christ ascending
steps.text: Arms open, robes billowing, Christ floats up into the light.

steps.title: The apostles
steps.text: Below, the apostles react: some kneel, some shield their eyes, some point. Every gesture is different.

steps.title: Two angels
steps.text: Two angels in white stand at right, telling the apostles Christ will return.

steps.title: Clouds and light
steps.text: Golden light breaks through dark clouds: heaven opening.

32168.file: John Singleton Copley - Mary and Elizabeth Royall - 25.49 - Museum of Fine Arts.jpg

steps.title: First look
steps.text: Mary and Elizabeth Royall, daughters of a wealthy Massachusetts family, painted by Copley around 1758, when he was about 20.

steps.title: The two sisters
steps.text: Close together, the older Mary at left, Elizabeth at right.

steps.title: The dog
steps.text: Elizabeth holds a small black dog, a classic symbol of loyalty.

steps.title: Satin
steps.text: Blue and cream satin, painted with brilliant highlights. The young Copley was already a master of fabric.

steps.title: The curtain
steps.text: A red curtain sweeps behind them, a grand backdrop for two young girls.

31586.file: John Singleton Copley - John Quincy Adams - 17.1077 - Museum of Fine Arts.jpg

steps.title: First look
steps.text: John Quincy Adams at 29, painted by Copley in London in 1796. He would become the sixth president of the United States.

steps.title: His face
steps.text: Young, confident, the eyes catching the light.

steps.title: The oval
steps.text: The portrait is painted inside an oval: a traditional format for a bust portrait.

steps.title: Stormy sky
steps.text: A dramatic sky behind his shoulder, more romantic than the plain backgrounds of Copley’s Boston years.

32060.file: John Singleton Copley - Nicholas Boylston - 23.504 - Museum of Fine Arts.jpg

steps.title: First look
steps.text: Nicholas Boylston, a rich Boston merchant, painted by Copley around 1769.

steps.title: The cap
steps.text: Instead of a wig, a soft velvet cap: fashionable informality for a gentleman at home.

steps.title: The silk banyan
steps.text: He wears a banyan, a loose silk robe imported from the East: a sign of wealth and worldly taste.

steps.title: The hand on the books
steps.text: His hand rests on books, showing him as a man of learning as well as trade.

steps.title: His face
steps.text: A shrewd, relaxed expression, painted without flattery.

steps.title: First look
steps.text: George Washington beside his horse, painted by Gilbert Stuart in 1806 for Boston’s Faneuil Hall.

steps.title: Washington
steps.text: Calm and upright, Washington stands like a statue in the middle of the action.

steps.title: The white horse
steps.text: His horse fills the right side, its head turned toward him.

steps.title: Smoke and sky
steps.text: Smoke and dark clouds behind recall the night in March 1776 when Washington fortified Dorchester Heights and forced the British to leave Boston.

31871.file: Gilbert Stuart - Bishop Jean-Louis Anne Magdelaine Lefebvre de Cheverus - 21.9 - Museum of Fine Arts.jpg

steps.title: First look
steps.text: Jean-Louis Lefebvre de Cheverus, the first Catholic bishop of Boston, painted by Gilbert Stuart in 1823.

steps.title: His face
steps.text: A gentle smile and a direct gaze: Stuart was famous for capturing personality.

steps.title: The cross
steps.text: A gold pectoral cross on a red cord, the sign of his office.

steps.title: The hand
steps.text: His hand rises in a speaking gesture, as if in conversation.

steps.title: The book
steps.text: A book at lower left: scholar and preacher.

32287.file: Gilbert Stuart - Colonel James Swan - 27.538 - Museum of Fine Arts.jpg

steps.title: First look
steps.text: Colonel James Swan, a Boston merchant and financier, painted by Gilbert Stuart in 1795.

steps.title: His face
steps.text: Ruddy cheeks and a powdered wig: Stuart builds the face with quick, fresh strokes.

steps.title: The blue coat
steps.text: A deep blue coat with a soft white cravat, the main colour notes.

steps.title: The red curtain
steps.text: Red drapery sweeps behind him, a classic backdrop.

steps.title: A dramatic life
steps.text: Swan later lost a fortune and spent over twenty years in a Paris debtors’ prison.

32288.file: Gilbert Stuart - Mrs. James Swan (Hepzibah Clarke) - 27.539 - Museum of Fine Arts.jpg

steps.title: First look
steps.text: Hepzibah Clarke Swan, wife of James Swan, painted by Gilbert Stuart in 1808.

steps.title: Her face
steps.text: Dark curls, a calm smile, a direct look.

steps.title: The lace veil
steps.text: A sheer lace veil falls from her hair, painted in a few light touches.

steps.title: Lace and black silk
steps.text: White lace against a black dress: Stuart loved this contrast.

32340.file: Gilbert Stuart - George Washington - 29.788 - Museum of Fine Arts.jpg

steps.title: First look
steps.text: George Washington, painted by Gilbert Stuart in 1810. It follows his famous ‘Athenaeum’ portrait, the face on the one-dollar bill.

steps.title: The face
steps.text: Stuart painted Washington from life in 1796 and kept painting copies for years. The original unfinished portrait is owned jointly by the MFA and the National Portrait Gallery.

steps.title: The mouth
steps.text: The tight-set mouth is often linked to Washington’s ill-fitting false teeth.

steps.title: Plain and dark
steps.text: No uniform, no background: just the man, in black, against a dark ground.

steps.title: First look
steps.text: Josiah Quincy, mayor of Boston, painted by Gilbert Stuart in 1824.

steps.title: His face
steps.text: Energetic, windswept hair, looking straight at us.

steps.title: The new market
steps.text: Behind him rises Quincy Market, the market building he championed for Boston, under construction from 1824.

steps.title: The plans
steps.text: In his hands, the building’s plans.

31260.file: John Singer Sargent - An Artist in His Studio - Google Art Project.jpg

steps.title: First look
steps.text: An artist in his cramped hotel room, painted by Sargent around 1904. The painter is his Italian friend Ambrogio Raffele.

steps.title: The painter
steps.text: Raffele sits hunched at left, working on a small canvas.

steps.title: The unmade bed
steps.text: Rumpled white sheets fill half the room: the studio is also where he sleeps.

steps.title: Paintings everywhere
steps.text: Landscape studies are propped and pinned around the room.

steps.title: White on white
steps.text: The sheets are a showpiece of whites: cream, blue-grey, gold. Sargent loved painting light on white fabric.

31959.file: John Singer Sargent - The Master and His Pupils - Google Art Project.jpg

steps.title: First look
steps.text: A painter and his pupils sketching by a mountain stream, painted by Sargent in 1914.

steps.title: The painters
steps.text: Small in the middle distance, the master and his students sit with their easels and parasols.

steps.title: The rocks
steps.text: Most of the picture is the stony stream bed, painted with quick, sure strokes.

steps.title: The forest
steps.text: Dark pine trees close the view at the top.

31976.file: John Singer Sargent - Low Tide at Cancale Harbor - 22.646 - Museum of Fine Arts.jpg

steps.title: First look
steps.text: Low tide at Cancale, a fishing port in Brittany, painted by the young Sargent in 1878.

steps.title: Beached boats
steps.text: Boats lie tilted on the sand, waiting for the tide.

steps.title: The far boats
steps.text: Out on the flats, more boats and figures, tiny in the haze.

steps.title: A figure in the sand
steps.text: At lower left, a figure lies in the sand.

steps.title: Light and air
steps.text: Pale sky, wet sand, white sails: Sargent at 22, already painting light like the Impressionists.

31955.file: John Singer Sargent - Robert de Cévrieux - Google Art Project.jpg

steps.title: First look
steps.text: Robert de Cévrieux, a young boy, painted by Sargent in 1879.

steps.title: His face
steps.text: Serious, a little shy, under a neat fringe.

steps.title: The dog
steps.text: Tucked under his arm, a small black dog, almost lost in his dark velvet suit.

steps.title: Red accents
steps.text: A big red bow and red stockings: two bright notes in a dark picture.

steps.title: The background
steps.text: Dark and loosely brushed, so the boy stands out.

31960.file: Rehearsal at the Cirque d'Hiver by John Singer Sargent.jpg

steps.title: First look
steps.text: An orchestra rehearsing in the Cirque d’Hiver, a circus building in Paris, painted by Sargent around 1879–80, almost all in black and white.

steps.title: Instruments
steps.text: Trombones, bows and music stands jut out at every angle: you can almost hear the noise.

steps.title: The players
steps.text: Musicians are dark smudges of paint, captured in a hurry.

steps.title: The circus seats
steps.text: Rows of empty seats curve at the top: it’s a rehearsal, not a concert.

steps.title: The inscription
steps.text: Sargent wrote at lower right where it was painted and signed his name.

steps.title: First look
steps.text: Washington on the night of December 25, 1776, before crossing the Delaware to attack Trenton. Thomas Sully painted it in 1819.

steps.title: Washington
steps.text: On a white horse, calm, looking back toward his troops.

steps.title: The soldiers
steps.text: Below, soldiers haul a cannon through the snow.

steps.title: The river
steps.text: In the distance, the icy river they will cross.

steps.title: The officers
steps.text: Officers on horseback wait at right, one pointing ahead.

steps.title: Too big
steps.text: Commissioned for North Carolina’s State House, the canvas turned out too big for its space, so it ended up in Boston.

31554.file: Thomas Sully - The Torn Hat - 16.104 - Museum of Fine Arts.jpg

steps.title: First look
steps.text: The Torn Hat, painted by Thomas Sully in 1820. The boy is his son, Thomas Wilcocks Sully.

steps.title: The torn straw hat
steps.text: A big straw hat, torn at the brim.

steps.title: Light through the tear
steps.text: Sunlight slips through the hole and lands on his cheek: that warm patch of light is the heart of the picture.

steps.title: His eyes
steps.text: Calm, direct, very childlike.

122064.file: William Michael Harnett - Still Life with Violin - 2000.2 - Museum of Fine Arts.jpg

steps.title: First look
steps.text: A still life with a violin, painted by William Michael Harnett in 1885. Harnett was a master of trompe-l’oeil, painting that fools the eye.

steps.title: The violin
steps.text: Every string, every curl of the wood looks real.

steps.title: Sheet music
steps.text: Curling pages of music with notes you could almost read.

steps.title: Delft jug
steps.text: A blue-and-white jug catches the light.

steps.title: Old books
steps.text: Worn books with a fanning page: things used and loved.

steps.title: The card
steps.text: A card tilted at the edge of the table, as if you could pick it up.

31974.file: William McGregor Paxton, The New Necklace, 1910.jpg

steps.title: First look
steps.text: A young woman tries on a new necklace while her friend looks on, painted by William McGregor Paxton in 1910.

steps.title: The necklace
steps.text: She holds it up to the light, the centre of everyone’s attention.

steps.title: The standing friend
steps.text: Her friend stands thoughtfully, hand at her chin.

steps.title: The pink jacket
steps.text: An embroidered Chinese jacket over a pale skirt: Boston taste for the exotic.

steps.title: The desk
steps.text: A fine desk at left, with an open drawer.

steps.title: Like Vermeer
steps.text: Soft light, quiet women, precious objects: Paxton deeply admired Vermeer.

31346.file: Edmund C. Tarbell - Girl Reading - 09.209 - Museum of Fine Arts.jpg

steps.title: First look
steps.text: A girl reading in a quiet room, painted by Edmund Tarbell in 1909, a leader of the Boston School.

steps.title: The reader
steps.text: Head bent over a book, completely absorbed.

steps.title: Window light
steps.text: Light pours in from the window at right and spreads across the room.

steps.title: The blue-and-white jar
steps.text: A Chinese jar catches the light, one of Tarbell’s favourite props.

steps.title: A bowl of fruit
steps.text: A small bowl on the floor: a still life inside the picture.

steps.title: Like Vermeer
steps.text: A woman, a window, silence: Tarbell, like Paxton, learned from Vermeer.
